rows.description: A young adult asks a friend how did that feel, not did you like it, and gets a fuller answer. Open, curious questions invite stories, while leading ones invite agreement.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 23–26

rows.description: A person is fired quick questions why did you do that, what were you thinking and feels attacked. The same content asked with softer tone and genuine curiosity brings better answers.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22

rows.description: A thoughtful colleague asks what would make this fail, or what am I not seeing. Such questions surface hidden risks and show respect for other viewpoints.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22

rows.description: A crying toddler quiets when held and spoken to softly, regardless of what was wrong. Before language, feeling accepted is the entire comfort needed.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A parent says you are sad because your friend left, and the child nods and calms. Naming a feeling helps a small child sort it and feel understood.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A child crying over a lost match is told it is just a game, stop crying. The child learns to hide feelings, not that they are small.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Wanting to be heard, not advised [Receiver]
rows.description: A teenager vents about a teacher and gets a list of solutions, so they stop sharing. Often the request is to be heard first, and advice is welcome only if asked.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 23–26

rows.description: A person says that sounds really hard, and then asks would you like ideas or just company. Validation first and asking permission to problem-solve respects both feeling and agency.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17

rows.description: Children arguing over a game push louder and repeat the same claim. Learning to state what the other person said before answering starts to change the pattern.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager in a quarrel says you always or you never and drags in old grievances. Absolutes provoke defence, and specific present issues keep the argument solvable.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
